proposals.before: When Emperor Ming took the throne, Zimin, son of the Prince of Yongyang, was left in his original fief and made to succeed the Prince of Yuan as his grandson-heir.
proposals.after: When Emperor Ming took the throne, Zimin, the Prince of Yongyang, was left in his original fief and made to succeed the Prince of Yuan as his grandson-heir.
proposals.reason: Chinese 永陽王子珉 is Prince Zimin of Yongyang; 子珉 is the given name, not son of another Yongyang prince.

proposals.before: When Emperor Ming took the throne, the Prince of Yongyang's son Min was kept in his original fief and made to succeed the Prince of Yuan as grandson-heir.
proposals.after: When Emperor Ming took the throne, Yongyang Prince Zimin was kept in his original fief and made to succeed the Prince of Yuan as grandson-heir.
proposals.reason: Chinese 永陽王子珉 names Prince Zimin of Yongyang; splitting 子珉 as son Min misreads the given name.

proposals.before: Again the third son of Prince Zhao of Wuling, Ye, Zitan, was made to continue the Prince of Yuan's line.
proposals.after: Again Zitan, the third son of Prince Ye of Wuling (posthumous title Zhao), was made to continue the Prince of Yuan's line.
proposals.reason: Literal English scrambles name order; 武陵昭王曄第三子子坦 is Zitan, third son of Prince Ye of Wuling.

proposals.before: He first served as Outside Attendant, then Supervisor of Attendants, Groom of the Heir Apparent, then Secretariat Gentleman and Interior Minister of Yuzhang—all declined.
proposals.after: He first served as Outside Attendant, then Supervisor of Attendants, Groom of the Heir Apparent, then Secretariat Gentleman; he was appointed Interior Minister of Yuzhang but declined.
proposals.reason: Chinese 不拜 applies only to 豫章內史, not to the prior offices; the literal wrongly says all were declined.

proposals.before: When the sage empress was in Heaven he personally received her entrustment; her words still ring in the ear, her virtuous voice still lingers—yet he insults Heaven's clarity, fears no injustice, and harbors a heart without a sovereign; the day he treads on frost has long been at hand.
proposals.after: When the sage sovereign was in Heaven he personally received his entrustment; his words still ring in the ear, his virtuous voice still lingers—yet he insults Heaven's clarity, fears no injustice, and harbors a heart without a sovereign; the day he treads on frost has long been at hand.
proposals.reason: 聖后 here means the late sage ruler (Emperor Ming) whose entrustment is cited, not an empress.

proposals.before: When the sage empress was in Heaven he personally received her entrustment; her words still ring in the ear, her virtuous voice still remains—yet he insults Heaven's clarity, fears not injustice, has a heart without a ruler; the day he treads on frost has long been coming.
proposals.after: When the sage sovereign was in Heaven he personally received his entrustment; his words still ring in the ear, his virtuous voice still remains—yet he insults Heaven's clarity, fears not injustice, has a heart without a ruler; the day he treads on frost has long been coming.
proposals.reason: 聖后 denotes the deceased sage sovereign; gendered pronouns in the literal should match.

proposals.before: Yaoguang sent Yuan Lisheng out to fight from the western gate; the Secretariat troops repeatedly fled north, and the army commander Sang Tian'ai was killed.
proposals.after: Yaoguang sent Yuan Lisheng out to fight from the western gate; the Secretariat troops were repeatedly defeated, and the army commander Sang Tian'ai was killed.
proposals.reason: In 臺軍屢北, 北 is the defeat sense of 敗北 ('routed'), not literal flight northward; the idiomatic field already translates it correctly.

proposals.before: Xiao Luan's sons and younger brothers were weak; Prince Bao of Jin'an had a crippling illness; therefore Yaoguang held Yang Province at the center and Yaoxin held the region west of the passes on the outside—power and influence were both in their house.
proposals.after: Xiao Luan's sons and younger brothers were young and weak; Prince Bao of Jin'an had a crippling illness; therefore Yaoguang held Yang Province at the center and Yaoxin held the region west of the passes on the outside—power and influence were both in their house.
proposals.reason: 弱小 means young/immature as well as weak; rendering only 'weak' omits the age sense that motivates entrusting power to Yaoguang and Yaoxin.

proposals.before: yet when ten sources of disorder filled the court, in truth it was only Queen Wen."
proposals.after: yet with ten able ordering ministers filling the court, in truth it was only Queen Wen."
proposals.reason: 十亂 means the classic 'ten ministers who bring order' (乱臣十人), not 'ten sources of disorder'.

proposals.before: yet when ten sources of disorder filled the court, in truth it was only Queen Wen."
proposals.after: yet when ten ordering ministers filled the court, in truth it was only Queen Wen."
proposals.reason: 十亂 is the Zhou allusion to ten capable ministers, not sources of disorder.

proposals.before: The next day he led his army toward the east of the city, sent the Daoist Deng Daoren into the city to bestow five hundred bolts of silk on the monks, and gave Qingyuan and Xuanzhi each trousers, jackets, and belt ornaments.
proposals.after: The next day he led his army toward the east of the city, sent the religious adept Daodeng into the city to bestow five hundred bolts of silk on the monks, and gave Qingyuan and Xuanzhi each trousers, jackets, and belt ornaments.
proposals.reason: 道登道人 is the monk/adept named Daodeng, not a surname Deng with title Daoren.

proposals.before: The next day he led his army toward the east of the city, sent the Daoist Deng Daoren into the city to bestow five hundred bolts of silk on the monks, and Qingyuan and Xuanzhi each received trousers, jackets, and belt ornaments.
proposals.after: The next day he led his army toward the east of the city, sent the Daoist adept Daodeng into the city to bestow five hundred bolts of silk on the monks, and Qingyuan and Xuanzhi each received trousers, jackets, and belt ornaments.
proposals.reason: 道登 is the personal/dharma name; 道人 is a religious epithet, not the name Deng Daoren.

proposals.before: He did not go to his commandery but was transferred to commander of military affairs in Yuzhou and the two commanderies Xiyang in Yingzhou and Runan in Sizhou, General Who Pacifies the Barbarians, and Governor of Yuzhou, with the staff unchanged.
proposals.after: He did not go to his garrison post but was transferred to commander of military affairs in Yuzhou and the two commanderies Xiyang in Yingzhou and Runan in Sizhou, General Who Pacifies the Barbarians, and Governor of Yuzhou, with the staff unchanged.
proposals.reason: 未之鎮 refers to not proceeding to the provincial garrison/post, not specifically a commandery.

proposals.before: The following year he was made Regular Attendant at the Imperial Secretariat and Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
proposals.after: The following year he was made Cavalier Regular Attendant and Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
proposals.reason: 散騎常侍 is the cavalier regular attendant, not an attendant at the Imperial Secretariat; the idiomatic rendering invents that office.

proposals.before: The next year he was transferred to Regular Attendant at the Imperial Secretariat and Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
proposals.after: The next year he was transferred to Cavalier Regular Attendant and Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
proposals.reason: Same error as the idiomatic field: 散騎常侍 is mistranslated as an Imperial Secretariat post.

proposals.before: In the third year Baohong was redesignated Marquis of Xiaocheng.
proposals.after: In the third year Baohong was redesignated to Xiaocheng.
proposals.reason: Chinese 改封宵城 does not specify Marquis; adding Marquis invents a rank not stated in the source.

proposals.before: His younger brother Baolan was made Duke of Jiangling and Baohong Duke of Runan, each with a fief of fifteen hundred households.
proposals.after: His younger brother Baolan was made Duke of Jiangling and Baohong was made Duke of Runan, each with a fief of fifteen hundred households.
proposals.reason: English fuses Baohong with the title as "Baohong Duke," omitting the parallel verb and obscuring the personal name.

decisions.reason: s0023 永陽王子珉 names the man as Prince of Yongyang with given name 子珉; s0024–s0025 confirm 子珉 is Emperor Wu’s son later titled 永陽, so “son of the Prince of Yongyang” invents a father–son split the Chinese does not make.

decisions.after: When Emperor Ming took the throne, Prince Zimin of Yongyang was kept in his original fief and made to succeed the Prince of Yuan as grandson-heir.
decisions.reason: The literal’s “Prince of Yongyang’s son Min” wrongly splits 子珉; the proposal correctly reunites the given name but “Yongyang Prince Zimin” is awkward—natural English is “Prince Zimin of Yongyang.”

s0027 武陵昭王曄第三子子坦 is Zitan, third son of Prince Ye of Wuling (posthumous 昭); the original’s “Prince Zhao of Wuling, Ye, Zitan” scrambles title, personal name, and son into a false sequence the proposal repairs.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 武陵昭王曄第三子子坦

decisions.reason: In s0043 the sequence ends 豫章內史，不拜; 不拜 scopes only to that last appointment, so “all declined” invents refusals of the prior offices the proposal correctly limits.

s0084 聖后在天…親受顧託 cites the deceased sage ruler’s final entrustment (here Emperor Ming), not an empress; “sage empress” and feminine possessives misgender the entruster the proposal restores as sovereign/his.
The same 聖后顧託 in the literal must be the late sage sovereign; matching masculine pronouns to that reading corrects the invented empress without altering the rest of the sentence.
臺軍屢北 uses 北 in the 敗北 sense “be routed,” not geographic northward flight; the proposal’s “repeatedly defeated” matches that military idiom (as the idiomatic field already does).

高宗子弟弱小 means the emperor’s sons and younger brothers were young as well as weak; literal “weak” alone drops the youth sense that motivates assigning power to Yaoguang and Yaoxin, which “young and weak” restores.
十亂盈朝 alludes to the Zhou “ten ordering ministers” (予有亂臣十人), with 文母 among them; “ten sources of disorder” reverses the classical sense the proposal correctly restores.
The literal repeats the same 十亂 misreading as disorder; “ten ordering ministers” recovers the Zhou allusion without inventing content.
道登道人 is the religious person named 道登 plus epithet 道人; “Daoist Deng Daoren” invents a surname Deng and mis-parses 道人 as a personal name the proposal correctly replaces with adept Daodeng.
The literal’s “Daoist Deng Daoren” makes the same parse error on 道登道人; “Daoist adept Daodeng” keeps 道人 as epithet and 道登 as the personal/dharma name.
未之鎮 means he did not proceed to take up the garrison/provincial post; rendering 鎮 as “commandery” invents a 郡 that the proposal’s “garrison post” correctly avoids.
散騎常侍 is Cavalier Regular Attendant; “at the Imperial Secretariat” invents an office the Chinese does not name, and the proposal restores the standard title.
The literal repeats the same 散騎常侍 mislabeling as an Imperial Secretariat post; Cavalier Regular Attendant is the accurate office name.
改封宵城 only redesignates the fief to Xiaocheng and does not state 侯; “Marquis of Xiaocheng” invents a rank the proposal rightly drops.
The original’s parallel ellipsis (“Baolan was made Duke of Jiangling and Baohong Duke of Runan”) already names both men and titles accurately; adding a second “was made” is stylistic only.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 弟寶覽爲江陵公，寶宏汝南公

claimRevisions.reason: Accepted r0011 shows English “Daoist Deng Daoren” came only from misparsing 道登道人; the religious-name claim remains valid with en corrected to Daodeng the religious adept while zh, id, subject, predicate, certainty, and evidence stay unchanged.
